title: Same Numbers, Different Answers
paragraphs: Utilitarianism, in the form developed by Jeremy Bentham and later refined by John Stuart Mill, holds that the right action is the one that produces the greatest overall happiness. Its appeal lies in its impartiality: each person's welfare counts equally, and no one's interests are privileged by rank or relationship. Yet a theory judged purely by outcomes invites an awkward question about the means used to reach them.

In 1967 the philosopher Philippa Foot described a runaway tram heading towards five workers, which a driver could steer onto a side track where it would kill one. Most people asked about such a case say that turning the tram is permissible. Judith Jarvis Thomson, who later gave the puzzle its name, added a variant in which the only way to save the five is to push a large stranger from a footbridge into the tram's path. Here, although the arithmetic is identical, a clear majority refuses.

Strict utilitarians can bite the bullet and insist that pushing is the right choice, treating the widespread reluctance as a bias to be overcome. Others appeal to the doctrine of double effect, an older principle distinguishing harm that is intended as a means from harm that is merely foreseen as a side effect. On this view the stranger on the bridge is used as a tool, whereas the worker on the side track is not. Neither response is free of difficulty, and the debate has continued for decades.

What the cases reveal, perhaps, is less a verdict on utilitarianism than a fact about moral thinking itself. Our judgements seem sensitive not only to how many lives are at stake but to how harm is brought about, and any credible theory must either explain that sensitivity or argue convincingly that it should be abandoned.
